title: Busan Between Stations
desc: When something terrible breaks loose inside Seoul Station, a snack vendor who has spent eleven years learning strangers' habits watches the morning commute turn into a nightmare — while a southbound KTX carries a father, a little girl, and a pink gift bag straight toward it.

chapters.title: Chapter One · The Last Cup of Coffee
chapters.byline: Seoul Station snack vendor · Concourse level · Dawn, moving toward morning

blocks.x: At 5:12, the station belongs to the people who clean it.

They push wide mops through the concourse in slow, practiced strokes, guiding the dirty water around the feet of the first commuters. They empty bins full of yesterday’s cups and damp tissues. They polish the glass doors, though every time the doors slide open a fresh breath of cold air clouds them again.
By six, the station belongs to people going to work.
By seven, it belongs to everyone who is trying to get somewhere before someone notices they are late.

I belong to the snack stall wedged between a pillar and the way down to the platforms. I open its metal shutters at five-thirty. The first one sticks halfway, so I lift it by the handle and lean my shoulder against the bottom until the track catches. I have done this every morning for eleven years. I know which hinge complains, which fluorescent strip takes a second to wake up, and how long the coffee machine needs before it can make a cup that doesn’t taste as if it came from a hot plastic pipe.
I know these things better than I know the people who pass my counter.

I know the man with the leather briefcase buys two coffees on Tuesdays, but only one on Thursdays. I know a woman in a red scarf always asks whether the red-bean buns are fresh and buys one even when I tell her they are yesterday’s. I know which schoolchildren come in groups and which ones wait until their parents turn away before they ask me for a second sweet.
People think the station is full of strangers. It isn’t. It is full of people you recognize without knowing their names.
That morning, the coffee machine coughs and sends half a cup across the counter.
“Not today,” I tell it.
The machine makes another small, mechanical groan.

I wipe up the coffee with a rag, rinse the rag in a plastic basin, then lay out the paper cups. I line them up with their rims facing the same way. A habit, nothing more. A little order for a place that never stays orderly for long.

Behind me, the television is showing a news anchor with the sound turned low. A caption crawls across the bottom of the screen: *Authorities respond to incident at medical facility. Public asked not to spread unconfirmed reports.*

Nobody watches. A pair of students stare at their phones. A businessman stands in front of the television while reading an entirely different story on his own screen. The station announcements swallow whatever the anchor is saying.

The morning is cold enough that people bring it inside with them. It clings to their coats and hair. The first train announcements come and go. Doors open. Doors close. Luggage wheels knock over the seams in the floor.
I put a tray of steamed buns beneath the warmer and watch the minute hand move.
At 6:21, a girl comes to the counter with a man in a dark suit.

She is small enough that she has to stand on the metal strip at the bottom of the stall to see the pastries properly. There is a folded gift bag tucked beneath her arm. The paper is pale pink, creased at one corner, its handles tied in a neat bow.
The man’s phone rings. He glances at the screen and steps half a pace away to answer it.
“Do you have anything without chocolate?” the girl asks.
“Red bean,” I say. “Sweet potato. Plain bread.”
“Which one is the best?”
“That depends on who’s asking.”
She smiles. Not much, but enough that it reaches her eyes. She studies the buns. Her father—or the man with her; I don’t know then—turns away from his call to look at her.
“Get whichever one you want,” he says.
She points to the red-bean bun.
I take it from the warmer, put it in a paper sleeve, and set it on the counter. The girl searches through the pocket of her coat. The man taps his card before she finds anything.
“Thank you,” she says.
“You’re welcome.”

Her companion is already looking at his phone again. He doesn’t seem cruel. He doesn’t seem angry. He looks like a man who has packed too much into a morning and is trying to make each minute fit inside the next one.
The girl looks past me, toward the departure board.
“Busan,” she says. “That’s our train.”
“That’s a long ride,” I tell her.
“I know.”
“Have you got something to do?”
She taps the gift bag with one finger. “I brought a present.”
“For someone in Busan?”
She nods.
I want to ask who, but the man ends his call and slips the phone away.
“We need to go,” he says.

The girl takes the bun and follows him. The gift bag bumps against her coat as they walk. She turns her head once, looking back at the stall, not at me exactly but at the warm light over the pastries. Then the crowd folds around them and they are gone.
I forget them for almost an hour.
At 6:48, the woman in the grey coat falls near the ticket gates.

She does not stumble first. She does not grab at anyone or cry out. One moment she is walking with the crowd, carrying a white shopping bag in her right hand. The next, the bag slips from her fingers and she drops to her knees.
Something inside the bag rolls away. An apple bumps along the polished floor and disappears beneath the edge of a bench.
A cleaner reaches her first. He is a thin man with a yellow safety vest and a mop wringer balanced on the cart behind him.
“Ma’am?” he says.
The woman’s head hangs forward. Her hair covers her face. People flow around them, glancing down as they go. One man steps over the fallen shopping bag. A woman pulls her suitcase closer to her legs.
The cleaner crouches and touches the woman’s shoulder.
She jerks so hard that the cleaner rocks backward.
I stop wiping the counter.

The man beside the gates raises his phone. Another person says something I can’t hear. The woman’s face lifts. Her mouth is open. She makes a wet, unsteady sound, like she is trying to cough something out of her throat.
The cleaner reaches for his phone.
Then the woman lunges.

The cleaner goes down on one knee. His cart tips. The mop handle clatters across the floor. People begin shouting—not all at once, not yet. The first shouts are uncertain, almost embarrassed. Someone tells the cleaner to get away from her. Someone else says she’s having a seizure.
I pick up the phone behind the counter.
My fingers miss the emergency number twice.
“Seoul Station security,” I say when someone answers. “At the gates. A woman’s down. She’s biting—”
I stop.

The woman’s face is pressed to the cleaner’s sleeve. The cleaner is trying to push her away with both hands. His yellow vest twists under her grip. There is a red mark on his wrist, then something darker.
A man in a business coat says, “Don’t touch her.”
He says it while moving closer to film.
A second cleaner runs in from the other side of the concourse. A security guard follows him. They grab the woman by her shoulders. She twists between them, spine bent, teeth snapping at the air.

The crowd has begun to thin in one direction and thicken in another. People are trying to see without being close. The ones farther away lift their phones. The ones nearby take a step back and then another. Nobody knows what to do, so they do the thing everyone else is doing.
A little girl cries. Someone tells her to be quiet.
I set the phone down.
“Stay away from her,” I shout, though the sound barely travels. “Get back.”
No one hears me. Or they hear me and don’t know why I should be listened to.
The guard catches the woman around the chest. She folds forward and bites his forearm. His cry cuts through the station. For half a second, every face turns toward him.
Then the concourse breaks open.

People run toward the platforms. People run from the platforms. A suitcase overturns. A man falls against the edge of my stall. Someone knocks over the rack of packaged snacks outside my shutter. Plastic bags skitter across the floor.
I pull the shutter down.
It catches halfway.
“Come on,” I mutter.

I lift it, shove it, and the metal slats grind down with a sound that seems louder than the shouting. The shutter reaches my waist and stops. Someone slams into it from the other side. I grab the bottom edge and push down with both hands.
A boy appears beneath it.
He has a navy school jacket and a blue backpack printed with little planets. He crawls on his elbows, his shoes scraping the floor. The shutter catches on one of the backpack straps.
“Keep going,” I tell him.
He kicks, tries to pull forward, and the bag holds him fast.
I look over his head.

The concourse is a blur of coats, arms, overturned bags. People are moving away from the gates, and something is moving against them. I can hear a man yelling for his wife. I can hear the amplified voice of a station announcement beginning, then stopping in the middle of a sentence.
“Leave the bag,” I say.
The boy hesitates.
“Leave it.”
I reach down and pull the strap free. The fabric tears. He slides under the shutter and scrambles behind the counter, nearly knocking over the coffee cups.
I let the shutter fall.
It slams shut between us and the station.
The boy sits on the floor with his back against the cabinet. His chest is heaving. He keeps looking at the narrow gap beneath the shutter, as if he expects someone to crawl through after him.
“Are you hurt?” I ask.
He shakes his head.
“What’s your name?”
He tells me, but the name is so small and lost beneath the noise that I don’t catch it.
“Your mother?”
He points toward the gates.
I kneel to look through the space beneath the shutter. Shoes rush past. One pair stops. Another pair stumbles. A hand appears on the floor, palm upward, fingers opening and closing.
I pull back.
The boy looks at me. His eyes are wide and dry.
“Don’t look,” I tell him.
I don’t tell him what I see. I don’t know if I can bear hearing it in my own voice.

The station announcement returns, this time in a different language. It asks passengers to remain calm and follow the instructions of station staff. The voice is calm because it is recorded. It has no idea what is happening here.

I move the boy deeper behind the counter. There isn’t much room. Cases of bottled water, cartons of bread, a box of paper cups. The back of the stall opens into a cramped service passage, but its door is kept locked from my side. I have the key on a ring with three others. My hands are shaking so badly that I drop it twice.
The boy hears the keys hit the floor.
“Are we going somewhere?” he asks.
“I’m opening the back.”
“Will my mother be there?”
I don’t answer.
I get the key in the lock. The service door opens a handspan, then catches on a stack of cardboard boxes. I push them aside. The passage beyond is dim, lit by a strip light that flickers at one end.

I could take the boy through it. There’s a delivery corridor leading to the loading bay. From there, perhaps, we can reach the staff exit. Perhaps there is still a station manager at the door. Perhaps the roads are safe.
“Come on,” I say.
He stands but looks back toward the shutter.
“My bag.”
It is caught halfway beneath the metal. The torn strap lies across the floor.
“I’ll get it.”

I ease up the shutter enough to reach through. My shoulders tense. My breath stops. I can see a plastic wrapper, a dropped shoe, the legs of people hurrying past. The backpack is just beyond my fingertips.
A body hits the shutter from the other side.
I jerk back. The metal rattles in its frame. The boy makes a sound and clamps both hands over his mouth.
I let the shutter drop again.
For a moment, I can’t move. My heart beats in my throat. I feel sweat beneath my collar, cold where the fabric touches my skin.
“Is it my mother?” the boy whispers.
“I don’t know.”
“I have to find her.”
“I know.”
“No, you don’t.”

He is right. I do not. I know the kind of worry that waits at home when a train runs late. I know the ache of listening for the gate to open after a family member’s shift. I don’t know what it is to be his age and hear the station turn into a place where your mother might be on the other side of a shutter.
I should keep him with me. I should take him through the passage and try to find help.
Instead, I do the first thing that makes sense to my frightened body. I point to the service door.
“Go that way. Keep going until you reach the loading bay. Find a uniform. Tell them where you came from.”
He stares at me.
“You’re not coming?”
I look at the shutter. I look at the narrow service passage. I look at the counter, the cash drawer, the shelves of food that are suddenly useless. The keys in my hand cut into my palm.
“I’ll come after you.”
This is a lie. I know it as I say it.
The boy’s face changes, just slightly. He knows too.
He goes anyway.
The service door closes behind him. I hear his shoes patter along the passage and fade. I stay with my hand on the latch until the sound is gone.
Then I sit on the floor.

The station is all noise beyond the shutter, but the sounds have begun to separate. Footsteps running. A man calling for someone. The heavy scrape of a metal barrier being dragged across tile. A series of sharp bangs from somewhere near the gates. The loudspeaker repeating the same announcement.
I hear one train depart.

The platform chime rises, bright and ordinary. The doors close. An engine pulls away. Through the small security monitor above the counter, I see a blur of silver moving past the platform windows. A southbound KTX, already in motion, its lit windows sliding by like a row of sealed rooms.

Somewhere in one of them, the father and the girl are still travelling toward Busan with a red-bean bun and a gift bag. I think of the girl’s small smile. I think of how she turned to look back at the warm stall.
The train disappears.
I put both hands over my ears, but the station’s sounds do not come from outside only. They are inside my chest now. I hear the boy’s question again. I hear my own answer.
*I’ll come after you.*

The television flickers back to life. Its volume comes up without warning. A reporter stands outside the station, speaking too quickly. The image breaks into squares and reforms. A caption runs beneath him: *Public transport service suspended amid violent disturbances.*
A second caption replaces it.
*Southbound KTX departure confirmed. Passengers advised to remain onboard.*

The camera cuts to a view from the platform. I see the back of the man in the dark suit. He is bending to speak to the girl. She holds the paper gift bag close to her chest. Then the view shakes, the feed stutters, and they vanish behind a pillar.
The television goes black.
I don’t know how much time passes. Ten minutes. Forty. The coffee machine switches itself off. The warmer clicks and cools. The buns inside turn from soft to damp.

I pull the blue backpack through the gap beneath the shutter when the pounding outside finally moves away. I drag it behind the counter. One strap is torn. There is a plastic dinosaur clipped to the zipper and a lunchbox inside with a tangerine rolling against its lid.
I set the bag beside me.

I don’t know the boy’s name. I don’t know whether he finds a uniform, whether his mother is looking for him, whether the loading bay is open. I don’t know if I have kept him alive or sent him somewhere worse.
I keep the keys in my fist until the teeth leave little half-moons in my skin.

When I stand, my knees hurt. I take one step toward the back passage and stop. I take another toward the shutter and stop there too. There is no right direction now, only doors I haven’t opened and sounds I don’t want to understand.
The emergency lights come on. Red light washes across the counter, the empty cups, the single bun left beneath the warmer. It makes the stainless steel look dark and wet.
I crouch behind the counter because I cannot think of anything else to do.

blocks.cap: Seoul Station, 07:12 — the concourse after the first fall.

blocks.x: **Where I am now:** Still inside my locked stall at Seoul Station, with a torn blue backpack beside me and the southbound train already gone.
